title: The dry bones (Ezekiel 37)
hook: a valley of bones rattles, joins, and breathes

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem written in the ashes of Jerusalem, and a line that held: his mercies are new, every morning. What did you thank God for first today? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Ezekiel was a priest who never got to serve in the Temple. He was carried off to Babylon in the first wave of exiles, years before the city fell, and he lived in a settlement by a river called the Chobar, a long way from home. That's where his visions came, and they were stranger than anyone else's. Wheels full of eyes. A scroll he was told to eat. And this one. The hand of the Lord takes hold of him and sets him down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones. Not a few. Very many, the text says. And very dry.
screen: `A PRIEST IN EXILE.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, AND VERY DRY.`

segments.voice: God walks him round about them, so he sees how many there are. Then God asks a question, and in the older English Bibles it reads: "Son of man, can these bones live?" It's a real question, and Ezekiel gives the only honest answer: O Lord God, thou knowest. So God tells him to preach to the bones. Ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. And while he's speaking there's a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin over them. And they lie there. Bodies, but no breath. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, and blow upon these slain, that they may live. And breath comes into them, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The whole chapter turns on one Hebrew word, ruach. It means breath. It means wind. It means spirit. Ezekiel uses it all three ways here, sometimes in the same sentence, and English has to pick one each time. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel. They're the people in exile saying our bones are dried up, our hope is lost. The vision is a promise that a people who thought they were finished would live and go home. Christians also hear in it the resurrection of the dead and the gift of the Spirit. The Church reads it at the Vigil of Pentecost and in Lent. Same valley. The bones don't argue their way back to life. They're spoken to, and then breathed into.
screen: `CAN THESE BONES LIVE? THOU KNOWEST.` · `BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.` · `RUACH: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT.` · `OUR HOPE IS LOST, THEY SAID.` · then, large: `COME FROM THE FOUR WINDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring something that feels dead into the valley. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that feels dried out. A friendship that went quiet. A hope you stopped mentioning. A part of your faith, or of yourself, that hasn't moved in a long time. Don't try to make it live. Just ask the question over it, the way God asked Ezekiel: can this live? And give Ezekiel's answer if you can't give another one: thou knowest. Then simply breathe. Notice that every breath in is ruach, the same word. If you pray, you can pray over it, as it is. The bell holds the time.
The dry bones. Ezekiel's vision of a valley of bones that come together and stand up when the breath of God enters them. Today's word.
Your line: can these bones live. Today, do one small thing for the dry thing you named: one message, one page, one step. Leave the rest to the breath. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones at the Vigil of Pentecost and on a Sunday in Lent, hearing in it the promise of resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: you're Ezekiel. God shows you a valley of very dry bones and asks: can these bones live? what do you say?
fork.reveal: he hands the question back to God. then God tells him to speak to the bones, and they rattle together.

original.note: Hebrew: breath, wind, spirit. Ezekiel 37 uses it all three ways.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spooky vision, or a children's song about bones.
what it means: a promise to exiles who said our hope is lost: God would raise them up and bring them home.
what a scholar hears: ruach, used for breath, wind and spirit in the same chapter; the bones are joined by the word and given life by the breath.

sources.quoted: Son of man, can these bones live?

notes: The carry 'can these bones live' follows the KJV of 37:3, quoted and cited as KJV; the Douay-Rheims reads differently (roughly 'dost thou think these bones shall live?'). Confirm whether a Catholic-path script should quote the KJV here, or paraphrase only.
Ezekiel among the exiles of 597 BC by the river Chobar (Kebar): confirm.
Ezekiel 37:1–14 as the Pentecost Vigil reading option and 37:12–14 on the 5th Sunday of Lent (Year A): confirm.
The KJV-style phrases 'O Lord God, thou knowest' and 'Ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord' are given as paraphrase, unquoted.
